summary:
Qatar criminalises consensual same-sex relations, with a sentence of up to three years available to Muslim and non-Muslim defendants alike, while Sharia permits a capital penalty that has never been imposed. The sources record no statute repealing or legalising this exposure and no legal change to the framework governing gender non-conformity.

Human Rights Watch reported on 24 October 2022 that Qatar's security forces arrested and abused LGBT people between 2019 and 2022, documenting six cases of severe repeated beatings and five cases of sexual harassment in police custody. Arrests took place in public places on the sole basis of gender expression and were accompanied by unlawful searches. Mistreatment was recorded as recently as September 2022, in the period when Qatar was preparing to host the 2022 World Cup under international scrutiny.

Transgender women interviewed by Human Rights Watch described punitive handling from the moment of arrest. One was detained for wearing makeup; officers made her wipe it off, kept the stained wipes as evidence, photographed her and shaved her head. Another was beaten until her lips and nose bled. All reported sexual harassment in custody, forced unlocking of their phones in order to identify other LGBT people, and conversion-therapy sessions imposed as a condition of release.

Detention was carried out in an underground prison in the capital, Doha. One woman spent two months in solitary confinement, and forced surgical removal of breast tissue was reported as a means of imposing physical detransition.

Beatings, torture and forced conversion therapy by police are documented independently of the individual cases above, and cultural norms are described as treating homosexuality and cross-dressing harshly. Visible non-conformity therefore carries exposure to both the criminal provisions and police practice described here.
tangentialFactors:
The police practice documented by Human Rights Watch is among the most severe recorded in the Gulf, and its continuation into September 2022 shows that it was not suspended while the country hosted a tournament under global scrutiny.

Public hostility to non-conformity predates the tournament period. A first-person essay by a gay Qatari man published by Doha News in 2016 drew extreme reactions that the writer described as jarring and as causing irreparable damage to mental health. Reporting in July 2018 recorded an entrenched taboo around homosexuality alongside no legal change, and commentary published ahead of the 2022 World Cup addressed the conduct visitors could expect to be held to. The harsh treatment of cross-dressing described in the sources is the element of that climate that bears directly on trans visitors rather than on gay and bisexual travellers alone.
localsOnly:
The criminal provisions and the documented arrest practice operate inside Qatar without regard to nationality: residents face the same exposure to arrest on the basis of gender expression, the same custodial conditions, and the same requirement to attend conversion-therapy sessions before release.

Police demand for phone access during custody has implications that extend past the individual detained, since the stated purpose was to identify other LGBT people known to them. Residents, and anyone whose contact list is held by a resident, fall within that risk.

The custodial conditions recorded by Human Rights Watch, including an underground facility in Doha and prolonged solitary confinement, apply to people held in the country indefinitely as well as to those transiting it.
outOfScopeNotes:
Rules governing passport and identity-document gender markers, and whether Qatari border or visa screening inspects them, are not addressed by these sources and remain unresolved here.

No information in the inventory covers entry refusal, deportation grounds, or any screening at the point of entry that could reveal a traveller's trans status. The same is true of access to gender-affirming healthcare, use of gendered facilities, hate-crime charging practice, and recognition of partners or marriages.

The counts of six beating cases and five sexual-harassment cases come from Human Rights Watch's interview sample rather than a national total. The sources do not establish how many people were interviewed overall or how many arrests based on gender expression occurred in Qatar in the same period.

Whether any provision of Qatari law offers anti-discrimination or legal-recognition protection to transgender people is not stated in these sources, and no such protection can be asserted or ruled out from this inventory.
